q: How do I calculate the GWP of a refrigerant blend like R-404A, R-407C or R-410A?
title: GWP of a refrigerant blend
short: Multiply each component's mass fraction by its GWP and add the results. R-404A is 44% R-125, 52% R-143a and 4% R-134a, so its AR6 GWP is 0.44 x 3,740 + 0.52 x 5,810 + 0.04 x 1,530 = 4,728. Use one IPCC report, AR5 or AR6, for every gas.
audience: Facility and cold-chain managers converting refrigerant invoices to CO2e

p: Use the nominal composition by mass from ASHRAE Standard 34 or the gas maker's safety data sheet. Fractions must add to 100 percent.
AR5 values are from Working Group I Chapter 8, Table 8.A.1; AR6 values from Chapter 7, Table 7.SM.7.

ul: Using mole fractions instead of mass fractions. Blend names give mass shares.
Mixing sets, such as AR4 values from an old label with AR6 values for other gases. Older AR4 based figures, such as 2,088 for R-410A, appear on many labels and quotes.
Treating a blend that contains R-22 or another HCFC as fully Scope 1. Split it: the HFC share goes in Scope 1 and the HCFC share is reported separately, outside the scope totals.
Taking a GWP printed on an invoice without checking which IPCC report it comes from.

example.title: Worked example: one year of top-ups at a cold store
lines: Top-ups: 20 kg of R-404A and 8 kg of R-407C
The AR6 total is about 20 percent higher for the same gas, so name the report you used

senseible: Senseible keeps refrigerant service and purchase invoices as evidence and calculates refrigerant CO2e when you give the gas and the kilograms charged into equipment; a gas purchase alone is not counted as leakage. The AR5 or AR6 choice changes only these gas figures, not its fuel and grid CO2 factors.
